challenges.title: Simple origami
challenges.description: Fold a sheet of paper (or a receipt, a flyer) into a simple shape: boat, crane, plane.
tips: Press each fold hard with your nail, the shape will hold much better.
Starting from a properly square sheet avoids half the problems.
The boat and the plane are the easiest ones to start with.

challenges.title: Recycled bookmark
challenges.description: Make a bookmark out of paper or cardboard you were about to throw away.
tips: A strip of roughly 5 by 15 cm is the ideal size.
Glue two layers together and it will last far longer.
Round off the corners, they survive much better inside a book.

challenges.title: A second life
challenges.description: Turn something headed for the trash into a small decoration.
tips: Look in your bin or recycling first, the idea will come from there.
A repurposed object doesn't need to be useful, just nice to look at.
Jars, tins and corks are the easiest things to repurpose.

challenges.title: Mini collage
challenges.description: Make a small collage from paper scraps or old magazines.
tips: Cut out a good ten pieces before you start gluing anything.
Lay it all out unglued first, move things around, then fix them.
Postcard size is plenty, no need to go big.

challenges.title: Origami crane
challenges.description: Fold a paper crane, the classic origami symbol. A tutorial is fine if you need one.
tips: Use a perfect square, the crane doesn't forgive a crooked sheet.
The bird base is the hard step, do it twice if you need to.
A failed first crane is a rite of passage, the second one goes better.

challenges.title: Improvised card
challenges.description: Make a spur-of-the-moment greeting card for someone, using whatever's on hand.
tips: Fold your sheet in half: the card already exists, now just decorate it.
Write the message before decorating, you'll manage the space better.
A simple repeated pattern beats one big failed drawing.

challenges.title: Mini herbarium
challenges.description: Pick up a leaf or flower outside and start a mini herbarium.
tips: Pick flat leaves, they dry far better.
Slide them between two sheets of paper inside a heavy book.
Note the date and place, that's what gives a herbarium its charm.

challenges.title: Box makeover
challenges.description: Decorate a box, jar, or pot you were about to throw away.
tips: Clean and dry the surface properly, otherwise nothing sticks.
Glued paper covers faster and more cleanly than paint.
One dominant colour gives a much tidier result.

challenges.title: Improvised bracelet
challenges.description: Make a bracelet or keychain with whatever's on hand.
tips: Measure your wrist with a piece of string before cutting.
Three braided strands are enough for something sturdy.
Thread, shoelace, ribbon, an old cut-up t-shirt: anything works.

challenges.title: Paper garland
challenges.description: Fold and cut out a simple paper garland.
tips: Fold your sheet accordion-style before cutting, that's the whole trick.
Never cut through the two outer folds or everything falls apart.
Simple shapes repeat much better than complicated ones.

challenges.title: A small origami animal
challenges.description: Fold a simple origami animal: a fox, a cat, a bird. A tutorial is fine if you need one.
tips: A square sheet, even cut down from an A4 page, works just fine.
The first folds matter most: take your time to line them up well.
Pick a model under ten steps to stay within the time given.

challenges.title: An improvised photo stand
challenges.description: Build a small stand to hold up a photo or card, using whatever you have on hand.
tips: A bent paperclip, a clothespin, or folded cardboard all work well.
Test that it stands up before decorating it.
A printed photo or a postcard works just as well as a drawing.

challenges.title: A hanging mobile
challenges.description: Assemble a small mobile by hanging a few found objects from a string or a branch.
tips: Three or four light objects are enough, no need to overload it.
Mix sizes and shapes so the mobile moves in an interesting way.
A branch picked up outside works just as well as a bought support.

challenges.title: A handmade label
challenges.description: Decorate a label for an everyday object: a jar, a drawer, a notebook.
tips: A piece of cardboard or thick paper is all you need as a base.
Something you use every day makes the label more useful.
Punch a small hole and attach it with string or thread.

challenges.title: A recycled pencil holder
challenges.description: Turn a can, a glass jar, or a milk carton into a pencil holder.
tips: Check for sharp edges before you start.
Paper, string, or paint are enough to cover it.
A slightly imperfect holder is still perfectly usable.

challenges.title: A fabric or paper pennant
challenges.description: Cut and decorate a small triangular pennant out of fabric or paper.
tips: A fabric scrap or an old colored sheet works perfectly.
One pennant is enough, no need for a whole string of them.
A simple pattern (stripes, dots) cuts faster than a detailed drawing.

challenges.title: A small folded pouch
challenges.description: Fold a sheet of paper into a small pouch or box to hold something tiny.
tips: An origami box tutorial (masu) gives a sturdy result in just a few folds.
Pick slightly thick paper, it holds its shape better.
Put something specific inside as soon as it's done, it gives it an immediate use.

challenges.title: A paper badge
challenges.description: Cut and decorate a small wearable badge, then attach a pin or paperclip to the back.
tips: Thin cardboard holds its shape better than plain paper.
A paperclip bent in half works just as well as a real pin.
A single pattern or word is enough, no need to overload the badge.

challenges.title: A decorated paperweight
challenges.description: Find a flat, heavy stone or object and decorate it to make a paperweight.
tips: A smooth, flat stone is easier to decorate than an irregular one.
Let the paint or glue dry before handling it.
A simple pattern holds up better over time than a very detailed drawing.

challenges.title: A cut-out doily
challenges.description: Fold a sheet of paper into several sections and cut shapes to reveal a doily pattern.
tips: Fold it fan-style or in a square first, like for a string of paper figures.
Cut small shapes along the folded edges, not the center, so it stays in one piece.
Unfold gently at the end, the pattern reveals itself all at once.
